subject: medicine
title: Anaemia of chronic kidney disease, erythropoietin, and hemodialysis access

steps.tx: Diminished renal parenchymal tissue mass compromises endocrine and excretory functions essential for normal erythrocyte production. Developing **anaemia of CKD** is characteristically normocytic and normochromic, emerging insidiously as the glomerular filtration rate falls below sixty millilitres per minute per one point seven three square metres. Impaired synthesis of erythropoietin by specialized interstitial peritubular fibroblasts in the renal cortex represents the predominant driver. Concurrently, systemic inflammation elevates circulating hepatic hepcidin, trapping iron within reticuloendothelial macrophages and starving developing erythroblasts of essential iron stores.
steps.say: Diminished functioning kidney tissue compromises endocrine signals essential for normal red blood cell production. Developing anaemia of CKD presents with normocytic normochromic red cells as filtration falls below sixty millilitres per minute. Impaired peritubular erythropoietin production represents the primary cause, compounded by hepcidin-mediated iron trapping within reticuloendothelial stores.

vis.alt: Diagram showing peritubular erythropoietin synthesis, bone marrow stimulation, and anaemia in CKD.
vis.caption: Renal peritubular fibroblast erythropoietin deficiency and systemic hepcidin elevation in CKD. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Targeted stimulation of erythroid progenitor survival and proliferation corrects chronic anaemic hypoxia in advanced renal disease. Administering recombinant **erythropoietin** or long-acting erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (such as darbepoetin alfa or methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta) is indicated when circulating haemoglobin falls below ten grams per decilitre, provided underlying iron stores are repleted. Clinical practice guidelines mandate titrating therapy to achieve and maintain a target haemoglobin between ten and eleven point five grams per decilitre. Deliberately normalizing haemoglobin above thirteen grams per decilitre increases risks of stroke and cardiovascular events.
steps.say: Targeted stimulation of bone marrow precursors corrects chronic anaemic hypoxia in advanced renal failure. Administering recombinant erythropoietin or darbepoetin is indicated when haemoglobin levels fall below ten grams per decilitre after correcting iron deficiency. Guidelines recommend titrating therapy to maintain haemoglobin between ten and eleven point five grams, avoiding excess stroke and thrombotic complications.

rows: Target 10.0 to 11.5 g/dL; coordinates iron transport

steps.tx: Adequate iron availability is mandatory to achieve optimal physiological responsiveness to exogenous erythropoietin stimulation. Differentiating **iron deficiency states** distinguishes absolute iron deficiency (depleted storage ferritin under one hundred micrograms per litre and transferrin saturation under twenty percent) from functional iron deficiency. In functional deficiency, elevated hepcidin blocks iron release despite abundant reticuloendothelial ferritin stores. Intravenous iron formulations (iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose, or ferumoxytol) bypass intestinal hepcidin blockades, delivering superior bone marrow delivery compared to oral iron supplements in advanced chronic kidney disease.
steps.say: Adequate iron availability is necessary to achieve optimal bone marrow response to erythropoietin therapy. Differentiating iron deficiency states distinguishes absolute deficiency from functional iron deficiency caused by high hepcidin levels. Intravenous iron formulations bypass gut absorption blocks, delivering reliable iron repletion in patients undergoing dialysis.

left.title: Absolute Iron Deficiency
points: True depletion of total body iron stores
Requires aggressive intravenous or oral iron loading

right.title: Functional Iron Deficiency
points: Iron trapped in macrophages by high hepcidin
Responds preferentially to intravenous iron therapy

steps.tx: Accumulation of diverse organic retention products normally cleared by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion produces multisystem toxicity in end-stage renal disease. Manifesting as **uraemia**, toxic retention solutes including guanidines, phenols, indoxyl sulfate, and beta-two microglobulin cause widespread cellular dysfunction. Symptoms include fatigue, anorexia, nausea, metallic taste, asterixis, peripheral neuropathy, and severe intractable pruritus. Critical manifestations warranting immediate life-saving dialytic intervention include uraemic pericarditis (presenting with friction rub and chest pain without typical ST elevations) and uraemic encephalopathy featuring profound confusion, seizures, or coma.
steps.say: Accumulation of organic retention products normally cleared by healthy kidneys produces multisystem toxicity in kidney failure. Manifesting as uraemia, toxic molecules cause anorexia, nausea, asterixis, and debilitating pruritus. Critical manifestations requiring emergency dialytic therapy include uraemic pericarditis with a pericardial rub, and severe uraemic encephalopathy featuring confusion and coma.

vis.alt: Clinical signs and multisystem organ involvement in the uraemic syndrome.
vis.caption: Multisystem organ toxicity and clinical manifestations of the uraemic syndrome. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Circulating uraemic toxins induce qualitative platelet dysfunction that manifests as mucocutaneous haemorrhage despite normal circulating platelet counts and normal standard coagulation profiles. Characterized as **uraemic bleeding**, toxins such as guanidinosuccinic acid inhibit platelet factor three activation and disrupt von Willebrand factor binding to platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors. The clinical hallmark is a markedly prolonged bleeding time with normal prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time. Urgent reversal prior to surgical procedures utilizes intravenous desmopressin (DDAVP), cryoprecipitate, or intensive hemodialysis sessions.
steps.say: Circulating uraemic toxins induce qualitative platelet defects causing bleeding despite normal platelet numbers and normal coagulation times. Characterized as uraemic bleeding, retention toxins impair platelet activation and adhesive binding. The diagnostic hallmark is a prolonged bleeding time with normal coagulation tests, treated before surgery with desmopressin or emergency dialysis.

right.title: Emergency Reversal Interventions
points: Desmopressin (DDAVP 0.3 ug/kg IV): Rapid onset (1 hr)
Cryoprecipitate: Transfuses concentrated vWF and fibrinogen
Haemodialysis: Clears dialyzable uraemic platelet toxins

steps.tx: Extracorporeal clearance of metabolic waste products and excess plasma fluid maintains homeostasis in end-stage renal failure. Performing **haemodialysis** circulates anticoagulated blood through a semipermeable synthetic hollow-fibre dialyzer counter-current to dialysate fluid. Diffusive mass transport down solute concentration gradients clears urea, creatinine, and potassium, while hydrostatic transmembrane pressure gradients drive convective ultrafiltration of excess fluid. Standard maintenance outpatient regimens deliver four hours of treatment three times weekly, achieving an adequate single-pool Kt/V clearance metric of one point two or greater per session.
steps.say: Extracorporeal clearance of metabolic wastes and excess fluid provides homeostasis in end-stage renal failure. Performing haemodialysis circulates blood through a synthetic dialyzer counter-current to dialysate fluid. Diffusive transport down concentration gradients clears urea and potassium, while hydrostatic pressure removes excess volume during four-hour sessions three times weekly.

nodes.label: Blood withdrawn from Vascular Access (300-450 mL/min)
Counter-current Diffusion + Ultrafiltration in Artificial Dialyzer
Purified blood returned to patient (Kt/V >= 1.2 per session)

steps.tx: Home-based renal replacement utilizes the patient's native peritoneal microvasculature as a semipermeable biological dialyzing membrane. Performing **peritoneal dialysis** involves instilling sterile dialysate containing hypertonic dextrose into the peritoneal cavity via an indwelling Tenckhoff catheter. Uraemic solutes diffuse down concentration gradients into the fluid, while glucose-generated osmotic pressure gradients draw excess fluid across peritoneal capillaries. Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) utilizes manual daytime fluid exchanges, whereas automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) employs a nocturnal cycler machine. Peritoneal dialysate infection (peritonitis) represents the principal technical complication.
steps.say: Home-based renal replacement utilizes the patient's peritoneal membrane as an endogenous biological filter. Performing peritoneal dialysis involves instilling dextrose-containing fluid into the abdomen through an indwelling catheter. Toxic solutes diffuse into the fluid while osmotic gradients remove excess water, with cloudy dialysate marking peritonitis as the main complication.

rows: 4 to 5 manual exchanges throughout the day
Continuous steady clearance; no machine needed

steps.tx: Creating a durable, high-flow subcutaneous vascular communication provides reliable circulatory access for repetitive maintenance hemodialysis needle cannulation. Constructing an **arteriovenous fistula** (AVF) involves direct surgical anastomosis of an artery to an adjacent native vein, most commonly connecting the radial artery to the cephalic vein at the wrist (Cimino-Brescia fistula). Arterial pressure arterializes the vein wall over six to eight weeks of maturation. Adhering to the rule of sixes confirms maturation: blood flow exceeding six hundred millilitres per minute, vein diameter over six millimetres, and depth under six millimetres.
steps.say: Creating a durable subcutaneous vascular conduit provides reliable access for repetitive haemodialysis cannulation. Constructing an arteriovenous fistula involves direct surgical anastomosis of an artery to a native vein at the wrist. Arterial pressure thickens the vein wall over several weeks, providing superior long-term patency and lower infection rates than artificial grafts.

nodes.label: Surgical Anastomosis: Radial Artery to Cephalic Vein
Rule of 6s: Flow >600 mL/min, Diameter >6 mm, Depth <6 mm
